newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: FEATURE - Cambodian health care reserved for the rich.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cambodian health care reserved for the rich.

text.p: At Salina, a booming plastic surgery clinic on a busy street corner in central Phnom Penh, Cambodia's health care crisis seemed a distant nightmare.
Well-dressed young men and women relaxed in the reception area, flipping through thick albums of before and after photos and admiring the results of recent eye surgeries, nose jobs and face-lifts.
In a nearby operating room heavy with the scent of surgical spirits, a deft surgeon unwrapped a razor blade and cut thin strips from the eyelids of Yen Chao, 30, to give her a more western visage.
"I had the surgery because I want to look more beautiful," Yen Chao said cheerfully when she awoke 20 minutes later.

For wealthier, urban Cambodians like Yen Chao, her $120 eye surgery, a nose job or general medical procedure may not be state-of-the-art, but it is fairly safe at the dozens of private clinics registered with the Health Ministry.
But for most people in Cambodia, where health care ranks among the worst in Asia, that kind of service is an unimaginable luxury.
In the decades-old Kossamak Hospital in southern Phnom Penh, four to five patients crowded each bare room on a recent weekend. Modern medical equipment was conspicously absent.
Two bandaged accident victims with bloody wounds called out from adjacent metal beds, but no one seemed to hear.
There is an average of one qualified doctor per 11,643 people in Cambodia, and one per 20,599 people in rural areas, according to 1994 government health statistics.
By contrast, Japan had roughly one physician for every 542 people as of December 1994, according to the Health Ministry.

Hospitals frequently lack well-trained personnel, modern facilities and equipment, and the medical school is struggling to end the widespread corruption of past years, when students paid for degrees without having to attend class or study for exams, health workers said.

Worse, the Ministry of Health's small annual budget of about $24 million is being raided for spending in other areas, such as defence, according to opposition Khmer Nation Party leader and former finance minister Sam Rainsy.
Last month he said the ministry had spent less than a third of the money allocated for the first seven months of 1996 -- a charge that has gone unanswered by Finance Ministry officials.
Health workers confirmed that some budgeted funds have not materialised as expected, and ministry staff have trouble staying motivated at a salary of between $12 and $20 per month.
"It is an issue of political power," said Vandine Or, deputy chief of health policy, planning and health information. "What can we do?"

There is some cause for hope, however. The ministry is launching an ambitious programme to strengthen the country's health care administration and service with assistance from the World Health Organisation, she said.
In addition, a variety of non-government organisations assist rural clinics with training and supplies.
But there is still a long way to go before the massive gap between health care for the rich and poor can be addressed.
"Much of Cambodia is having to start its medical system from scratch," said Kimberly Baldwin Radford, coordinator of public health projects for the Adventist Development and Relief Agency Cambodia.
"It's scary. There's only a basic knowledge of treatment in much of the country," Radford said.
The hospital where she works, in the central province of Kompong Thom, is typically overrun with chickens and pigs, and the surgical tables are covered with plastic shelf liner.
It is a far cry from the polished floors of the Salina clinic, where for those who can afford it, money buys not just health but sometimes happiness.
"We have up to 40 operations a week," said clinic owner Heng Yong. "People see the results and feel beautiful."
